proof.criterion: The architect's second question: the body change orders the test's own setup and does not hide a product race.
proof.surface: The code that opens a round, read against what the test drove.
proof.command: read openPodUpdate's posting, reconcileIssuePodUpdate's gone-pod branch, lostClaims and memberOf, and the shape comparison in sandbox/drift.go.
proof.observed: The race the test hit is real but is the rig's, not the daemon's. openPodUpdate posts PodUpdateOpen to each blocking claim through s.supervisor.post, and each machine writes its own round when it handles that post, so for a moment a claim is not yet a member (memberOf reads UpdateRound and UpdateLeftRound). The test drove rig.tickBackIn in that moment, which rewrites every claim's locator in the snapshot synchronously, so the claims recorded the replacement pod microseconds after the round was posted and before the tester's write landed: lostClaims was empty, the pod-went branch was skipped, and the sweep opened a round over the replacement pod. A real daemon cannot reach that state by this path, because the two events it needs are orders of magnitude apart: the round's write lands in milliseconds, while a claim comes to record a different pod only after a replacement completes -- Sandbox suspend and recreate, schedule, image pull, launcher start, registration -- which is tens of seconds at best. Nor would the opened round be wrong if it happened: a pod the runtime has just built carries the current shape, which is what shapeDrift compares against, so no round opens over it unless the configuration moved again, and then opening one is correct. The one path that could delay a write materially is a machine held in a long decision (a Resume can hold one for minutes, which is why roundView reads the published view), and a claim whose round-write has not landed was never asked and never told to push, so it is not a member of the round and the report does not name it -- which is the design the record rule states, and the same silence a pod that dies with no round open already gets. So: setup ordering, not a hidden product defect. I record the long-decision path as the one I would re-examine if the report is ever asked to cover claims the round never reached.
proof.negativeControl: The implementer's own note is the control that the ordering matters to the test: with the extra wait removed the sweep opens a round over the replacement pod and the worker is sent a stray ask, which the unchanged assertion catches.

notes: The pod's PostgreSQL cannot drop a test database cleanly, and it is worth the next round knowing. The harness's teardown terminates the backends of the database it drops, which needs pg_signal_backend; the role every server here offers (legion_test) is not a superuser and cannot grant it to itself, so the drop fails with SQLSTATE 42501, the database is left behind, and the failure is charged to whichever test was tearing down. I met it first on the pod's shared server and then on a server of my own, where 76 databases had accumulated by the end of the run, and it is why I judge every run by its non-teardown messages. It reddens a different test each run and is not this branch's.
